title: The Deaf and the Mute
summary: Whatever lies in the mind's range, scripture, book and rosary, is ālā jālā; the innate cannot be spoken, so the guru instructs in vain, and the song ends with a mute guru and a deaf disciple (on an emended reading of 4b) and the Jina's jewel unfolding as a mute is instructed by the deaf. Munidatta reads the refrain as showing how hard the innate is to reach, since it lies beyond the body, speech and mind of ordinary people. He takes the Jina's jewel as the fourth joy and likens the true guru to a deaf man who makes a mute understand by signs.

lines.gloss: whatever · mind · range (gocara; in the range, or of the range) · ālā (sham? tangle?) · jālā (net? tangle?)
lines.en: Whatever lies in the [range of the mind]{manogocara} is [ālā jālā]{ala-jala}:

flags.note: ālā jālā is kept in source form (ala-jala, keep-source-first-gloss). Its sense is uncertain: a jingling pair suggesting a tangle or a sham (compare Hindi āl-jāl, 'rubbish, muddle'; jālā recalls jāla, 'net'). Munidatta puts 'the net of all concepts' in its place without glossing the word (cp.40.m2); the Tibetan line has mig 'phrul 'dra, 'like a magic show'. Neither reading is put into the line.

goera taken as locative ('in the range'), with ālā jālā as predicate: 'whatever lies in the range of the mind is ālā jālā'. If goera is genitive (-era), the line is a noun phrase: 'whatever ālā jālā of the mind's range', with 1b in apposition. The Tibetan line makes it a statement (gang zhig yid kyi spyod yul mig 'phrul 'dra).

lines.gloss: scripture · book · rosary (iṣṭa 'chosen deity' or 'desired' + mālā 'garland') · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: The Tibetan line reads lung dang po ste brdzun gyi phreng ba yin, 'scripture and po ste (probably pothī, 'book') are a garland of falsehood': the rosary becomes brdzun gyi phreng ba and the line a statement that these things are false. The Bengali has three nouns and no verb; the draft keeps the bare list.
Shastri prints the refrain cue dhru after couplet 1 as well, although the refrain is couplet 2 (Munidatta names couplet 2 the dhruvapada, cp.40.m3). The cue is not translated.

lines.gloss: say! · how · innate · to be spoken (verbal noun in -bā) · goes (with the verbal noun: can be)
lines.en: Say, how can the [innate]{sahaja} be spoken,

flags.note: Shastri prints bola bā jāya; read here as one verbal noun, bolabā, with jāya ('goes') as a passive or potential: 'can be spoken'. The Tibetan line agrees in sense (ji ltar smra bas lhan skyes brjod par nus, 'how can the innate be expressed by speaking'). bola here is the verb 'speak', not the code word bola of song 18.

lines.gloss: body-speech-mind · of which, in which · not · enters, fits, is contained
lines.en: where [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta} do not enter?

flags.note: jasu ṇa samāya: 'in which (body, speech and mind) do not enter' or 'are not contained'. Munidatta has nāntarbhavati, 'is not included' (cp.40.m3). Taking body, speech and mind as the container ('which body, speech and mind cannot hold') is grammatically harder, since kāavākcia is the subject and jasu the relative.

lines.gloss: in vain (or falsely) · guru · instructs · disciple

flags.note: āle: 'in vain' follows Munidatta, who takes it as Sanskrit alam glossed niṣphalam, 'fruitless' (cp.40.m4). The Tibetan line and comment take it as 'false' (bla mas brdzun gyi thabs kyis, 'the guru by false means'; bden pa ma yin pas, 'with what is not true'), as if from alīka. 'Falsely the guru instructs the disciple' is the alternative. The Tibetan also adds thabs, 'means', which the Bengali lacks.

lines.gloss: beyond the path of speech · will tell, is to be told · how, why
lines.en: how will he tell what is [beyond the path of speech]{vakpathatita}?

flags.note: kāhiba is a future or gerundive of kah-, 'tell'; the subject, left implicit, is taken to be the guru of 3a (Munidatta: 'by what means is it to be told by the guru?', cp.40.m4). kīsa can be 'how' or 'why'; 'how' agrees with Munidatta (kiṃ kṛtvā) and the Tibetan (ji ltar smra).

lines.translit: je tai bolī te tabi ṭāla
lines.gloss: what · so, therefore · is said · that · all (?) · ṭāla (unreal? false? evasion?)
lines.en: So whatever is said, all of it is [ṭāla]{tala};

flags.note: ṭāla is kept in source form and linked to the existing entry ṭāla (tala), made for song 33's ṭālata, because Munidatta glosses this word the same way: ṭālanam asadrūpam, 'a ṭālana, of unreal form' (cp.40.m5). The Tibetan line has brdzun, 'false' (gang de smra ba de dang de rnams brdzun). A translated alternative: 'all of it is false' (or 'a sham'; compare perhaps Bengali and Hindi ṭāl-, 'put off, evade'). Whether song 33's ṭāla, apparently a place, is the same word is doubtful.

tabi is unclear. Munidatta's 'all that' (tat sarvaṃ, cp.40.m5) and the Tibetan 'those and those' (de dang de rnams) suggest 'all', perhaps for sabi; 'then' (compare Bengali tabe) is possible. Munidatta's lemma for the couplet reads tejai, not je tai.
tai taken as 'so, therefore' (compare Bengali tāi), following Munidatta's tasmāt (cp.40.m5); 'by you' or 'of it' are possible. bolī taken as passive, 'is said', with Munidatta's bhaṇyate.

lines.gloss: guru + bodha (printed; 'understanding, teaching'; read boba, 'mute') + se ('that, he') · disciple · deaf

flags.note: Emended. Shastri prints gurubodhase; the draft reads guru boba se, 'the guru is mute, that disciple deaf', taking ধ (dha) as a slip for ব (ba), letters easily confused. For: Munidatta says the vajra guru too is 'possessed of poverty of words' in this dharma and his disciple heard nothing (cp.40.m5), and the reading pairs mute and deaf as 5b does. Against: the printed text, and the Tibetan line, bla ma'i thabs kyis slob ma 'khrul bar byas, 'by the guru's means the disciple was made confused'. Translating the print: 'at the guru's teaching the disciple is deaf'. 'mute' is left without muka markup, since it renders a conjecture and the printed বোধ should not be recorded as a form of muka.
kāla is 'deaf' (compare Bengali kālā), filed under badhira, not kāla 'time, death' (the glossary's kala, from song 1) or 'black'. The Tibetan has 'khrul, 'confused, deluded'.

lines.translit: bhaṇai kāhnu jiṇa raaṇa vikasai sā |
lines.gloss: says · Kāhnu · Jina · jewel · blooms, opens out · so (answering jaisā, 'as', in 5b)

flags.note: The Tibetan line has kAh+Nas rgyal ba'i rin chen ji ltar smra, 'how can Kāṇha speak the Jina's jewel?': a question, with 'speak' where the Bengali has vikasai sā, 'unfolds so'. The draft follows the Bengali.

vikasai (Sanskrit vikasati) is used of flowers opening and of light spreading: 'unfolds' is chosen to cover both; 'blooms' or 'shines out' are alternatives. Munidatta renders it tanoti, 'spreads' (cp.40.m6). sā is taken as 'so', answering jaisā at the end of 5b; it could also be the pronoun 'it'.

lines.gloss: by the deaf · mute · instructed · as, like
lines.en: as the [mute]{muka} is instructed by the [deaf]{badhira}.

flags.note: The Tibetan line reverses the roles: lkugs pas 'on par smra ba ji bzhin no, 'just as the mute speaks to the deaf'. In the Bengali kālem̐ ('by the deaf', instrumental) is the agent and boba the one instructed, as in Munidatta's simile, where the deaf man makes the mute understand (cp.40.m6).
saṃbohia is 'instructed, made to understand' (Sanskrit saṃbodhita; Munidatta's saṃbodhana, cp.40.m6), not 'awakened'. kālem̐ is filed under badhira, 'deaf', not time or death.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung. Mālasī-gavuṛā joins mālasī and gavuṛā; the Tibetan heading treats it as one name, mA la sa'i go Da la, 'the go Da la of mA la sa', and calls the piece the song (glu dbyangs) of nag po spyod pa'i zhabs, Kāṇha.

In Shastri's text the attribution kāhnupādānāṃ, 'of Kāhnupāda', is written before the first line. It is not part of the verse and has been removed from 1a. The heading line names only the rāga, so the poet is not added to the English heading here.

Munidatta introduces the song: Kṛṣṇācārya, delighted with innate joy (sahajānanda), sets it forth (cp.40.m1). The Tibetan has nag po glu dbyangs zhabs, 'Kāṇha of the songs', satisfied with innate joy, speaking in great delight.

ālā jālā is kept in its source form: a jingling pair of uncertain sense, perhaps 'tangle' or 'sham' (compare Hindi āl-jāl, 'rubbish, muddle'; jālā recalls jāla, 'net'). The same āl- may lie behind āle, 'in vain' or 'falsely', in 3a. maṇa goera is the mind's range (Sanskrit manogocara): whatever thought can reach.

Munidatta paraphrases the line as 'whatever is the range of the mind and the horse of the senses (as Shastri restores the text), the whole net of concepts' (sakalavikalpajāla). He puts the net of concepts where the song has ālā jālā but does not gloss the word itself. The Tibetan comment agrees: the range of mind and senses is the net of thought and concept (rtog pa dang rnam par rtog pa'i dra ba) (cp.40.m2).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads gang zhig yid kyi spyod yul mig 'phrul 'dra, 'whatever is the mind's range is like a magic show': it renders ālā jālā as a likeness to illusion, using mig 'phrul, its usual word for a conjuring display (indrajāla).

Scripture (āgama), book (pothī, a manuscript, in eastern India usually palm-leaf folios) and rosary (iṣṭāmālā, a string of beads for counting recitations; iṣṭa may mean the chosen deity) are the equipment of learned and ritual religion. The source leaves open whether they are examples of the ālā jālā or further things in the mind's range; so does the draft.

Munidatta adds 'or the knowledge of scripture, mantra, treatises and the like, and all that', so his list has mantra about where the song has the rosary, though he does not connect the two. He then begins a verse, 'scripture, Veda, Purāṇa…' (āgama vea purāṇe), and breaks it off (cp.40.m2).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads lung dang po ste brdzun gyi phreng ba yin, 'scripture and po ste are a garland of falsehood'. po ste is probably a transcription of pothī (compare po ti, 'volume'); the rosary becomes brdzun gyi phreng ba, 'garland of falsehood', and the line a judgement that these things are false. The Bengali is a bare list of three nouns.

Shastri prints the cue dhru after couplet 1 as well as after the refrain and the later couplets. Munidatta names couplet 2 the refrain (dhruvapada, cp.40.m3) and counts couplets 3 and 4 as his second and third padas (cp.40.m4, cp.40.m5), so the cue after couplet 1 is probably a slip. It is not translated.

Munidatta says that with the refrain the poet sets forth how hard the innate is to reach (sahajadaurlabhya): how can the innate, the unsurpassed knowledge, be spoken, the innate in which the body, speech and mind of ordinary people are not contained? He then quotes a dohā of Tilopāda: Tilopa says self-awareness is the fruit of the tantra, and what is hidden in the mind's range is not the ultimate. Its opening, jo maṇa goara, echoes the first words of the song (cp.40.m3).

bhaṇa is the imperative 'say'. Shastri's text of Munidatta's paraphrase begins ataeva vedaḥ kathaṃ…, 'therefore how can the Veda…'; vedaḥ is probably a slip for vada, 'say', rendering the song's bhaṇa. The Tibetan comment read it as the Veda (rig byed du, 'in the Veda') (cp.40.m3).

Munidatta's Sanskrit says the body, speech and mind of ordinary people are not contained (nāntarbhavati) in the innate. The Tibetan comment has no negative: the innate is that in which the body, speech and mind of ordinary beings dissolve (thim par gyur pa) (cp.40.m3). The Tibetan line keeps the negative (lus ngag yid la gang du mi 'jug go).

āle: Munidatta's lemma reads alem, and he takes it as Sanskrit alam, 'enough', glossed niṣphalam, 'fruitless': the guru gives instruction to the disciple in vain (cp.40.m4). The Tibetan line and comment take it as 'false' (bla mas brdzun gyi thabs kyis, 'the guru by false means'; bden pa ma yin pas, 'with what is not true'), as if from Sanskrit alīka, 'false'. The draft follows Munidatta. uesai is 'instructs' (Sanskrit upadiśati).

Munidatta counts this couplet as his second pada, on the nature of reality (tattvasvarūpa). The innate is not something known through talk, he says, so by what means could the guru tell it? He quotes Saraha: na taṃ vāe guru kahai, 'the guru does not tell it in words'; the Tibetan of the quotation has de med bla mas ji ltar smra, 'without that, how can the guru speak?' (cp.40.m4).

ṭāla is kept in its source form: a word of uncertain sense. Munidatta renders it ṭālanam asadrūpam, 'a ṭālana, of unreal form' (cp.40.m5), the same gloss, 'unreal form', that the glossary's ṭāla entry records for ṭālata in song 33. The Tibetan line (gang de smra ba de dang de rnams brdzun) and comment (brdzun te rang bzhin bden pa ma yin pa) have 'false', 'not true by nature'. Perhaps compare Bengali and Hindi ṭāl-, 'put off, evade' (Bengali ṭālbāhānā, 'prevarication'): what is said would be an evasion.

Munidatta's lemma for this couplet reads tejai, against the song's je tai. His paraphrase, 'therefore whatever is said of the innate … all that' (tasmāt … yad yad bhaṇyate sahajaṃ tat sarvaṃ), suggests tai, 'so, therefore', and tabi, 'all'. His bhagavati(ti) mātragatyā is obscure; the Tibetan comment's tshig tsam, 'mere words', suggests something like bhaṇitimātra-, 'by way of mere speech' (cp.40.m5).

Shastri prints gurubodhase as one word. As printed it gives something like 'at the guru's teaching (bodha, 'understanding, teaching') the disciple is deaf'. The draft reads boba, 'mute', for bodha (ব for ধ): guru boba se sīsā kāla, 'the guru is mute, that disciple deaf'. Munidatta supports this: the vajra guru too is, in this dharma, 'possessed of poverty of words', and because nothing is said his disciple heard nothing (cp.40.m5). The Tibetan line does not: bla ma'i thabs kyis slob ma 'khrul bar byas, 'by the guru's means the disciple was made confused'.

kāla here is 'deaf' (compare Bengali kālā), not kāla, 'time, death', or kālā, 'black'. In 5b kālem̐ is its instrumental, 'by the deaf'. The Tibetan's 'khrul, 'confused, deluded', may reflect another reading or understanding of the word.

Munidatta asks what kind of Jina-jewel this is and answers with a play on the word: it spreads (tanoti) delight (rati), endless unsurpassed bliss, and so it is a jewel (ratna); it is to be understood as the fourth joy (caturthānanda) (cp.40.m6). His tanoti, 'spreads', stands for the song's vikasai. The Tibetan comment has the jewel so called because its bliss is vast (rgya chen po).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads kAh+Nas rgyal ba'i rin chen ji ltar smra, 'how can Kāṇha speak the Jina's jewel?'. Where the Bengali says the jewel unfolds (vikasai sā), the Tibetan has a question about speaking it, echoing 3b (ngag gi lam nas 'das pa ji ltar smra).

The closing image is a mute instructed by a deaf person: teaching where one cannot speak and the other cannot hear. saṃbohia is 'instructed, made to understand' (Sanskrit saṃbodhita), not 'awakened'; Munidatta's simile has saṃbodhana in the same sense, done by signs and the like (cp.40.m6).

Munidatta opens his comment on the last couplet with 'so he too is deaf' (so 'pi ca badhiraḥ), then gives the simile: as a deaf man makes a mute understand by signs and the like, so the true guru, from afar, spreads great bliss in the disciple by the power of his own delight. He closes with Iuṛīpāda's 'near or far' (adūre dūre vā) (cp.40.m6). In the simile the deaf one stands for the true guru and the mute for the disciple, a correspondence made by 'as … so', not an explicit gloss. In his comment on 4b the guru is the one without words and the disciple the one who hears nothing (cp.40.m5), so the roles shift between the two couplets.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads lkugs pas 'on par smra ba ji bzhin no, 'just as the mute speaks to the deaf', reversing the Bengali, where kālem̐, 'by the deaf', is the agent. The Tibetan comment has the same order: by signs and the like the mute's understanding is conveyed to the deaf ('on pa la brda la sogs pas lkugs pa'i rtogs pa smra bar byed do), against the Sanskrit, where the deaf instructs the mute (cp.40.m6). The Tibetan thus keeps through the last line the roles of Munidatta's comment on 4b: the guru unable to speak, the disciple unable to hear (cp.40.m5).

termsOmitted.reason: 'mute' in 4b renders the conjectured boba (Shastri prints গুরুবোধসে); it is left unmarked so that the printed বোধ is not recorded as a form of muka. Not a detected hit; listed for the reviewer.
Tibetan only: the Tibetan line has mig 'phrul 'dra, 'like a magic show', where the Bengali has ālā jālā, which is kept in source form (ala-jala). Noted as a witness reading.
Tibetan only: thabs, 'means', is added by the Tibetan line (brdzun gyi thabs kyis); the Bengali has no word for it.
Tibetan only: bla ma'i thabs kyis, 'by the guru's means'; the Bengali (gurubodhase, read guru boba se) has no word for 'means'.

questions: 4b: I emended gurubodhase to guru boba se, 'the guru is mute, the disciple deaf', on the strength of Munidatta's paraphrase (the guru 'poor in words', the disciple hearing nothing, cp.40.m5) and the easy confusion of ধ and ব. The printed text and the Tibetan ('by the guru's means the disciple was made confused') are against it. Keep the emendation, or translate the print ('at the guru's teaching the disciple is deaf')? If it is kept, I left 'mute' in 4b without muka markup so that the printed বোধ is not recorded as a form of the term. Should it be marked?

4a: I kept ṭāla in source form and linked it to the song 33 entry (tala), because Munidatta gives it the same gloss, asadrūpa, 'unreal form' (cp.40.m5). Is it the same word? Or should 4a translate it: 'false' (with the Tibetan brdzun), 'a sham', or 'an evasion' (compare Bengali ṭālbāhānā)? If the link stands, the entry needs the forms টাল (oben) and টালন (san) and a mention of song 40.
3a āle: 'in vain' (Munidatta: alam, glossed niṣphalam, cp.40.m4) or 'falsely' (the Tibetan brdzun)? I chose 'in vain'.
5a: is 'unfolds' right for vikasai? 'Blooms' keeps the flower verb, and 'shines out' suits a jewel. I also took sā as 'so', answering jaisā in 5b. Do you agree?

1a: I took goera as locative, with ālā jālā as the predicate ('Whatever lies in the range of the mind is ālā jālā'). The genitive reading would give a noun phrase, 'whatever ālā jālā of the mind's range', with 1b in apposition. Which do you prefer?
Heading: the attribution kāhnupādānāṃ stands before the song but outside the heading line, so I left the poet out of the English heading. Should '· Kāṇha' be added, as in headings that name the poet?

For the woven commentary: in m3, vedaḥ is probably vada, 'say' (glossing bhaṇa), and in m5, bhagavati(ti) mātragatyā is probably bhaṇitimātra-, 'mere speech' (the Tibetan has tshig tsam). If so, the tx-veda hit in m3 and the p-bhagavati hit in m5 are spurious. Can you confirm before those segments are woven?
Shastri prints dhru after couplet 1 as well as after the refrain (couplet 2). I treated it as a slip and did not translate it. Is that right?
